orig_text:
The Speaker notifies the Listener that it has finished sending a
   Virtual File by sending an End File (EFID) command.  The Listener
   replies with a positive or negative End File command and has the
   option to request a Change Direction command from the Speaker.
 
   1. Speaker  -- EFID ------------> Listener   End File
               <------------ EFPA --            Answer YES
 
   2. Speaker  -- EFID ------------> Listener   End File
               <------------ EFPA --            Answer YES + CD
               -- CD -------------->            Change Direction
      Listener <------------ EERP -- Speaker    End to End Response
               -------------- RTR ->            Ready to Receive
      Listener <------------ NERP -- Speaker    Negative End Response
               -------------- RTR ->            Ready to Receive
               Go to Start File Phase
 
   3. Speaker  -- EFID ------------> Listener   End File
               <------------ EFNA --            Answer NO
correct_text:
The Speaker notifies the Listener that it has finished sending a
   Virtual File by sending an End File (EFID) command.  The Listener
   replies with a positive or negative End File command and has the
   option to request a Change Direction command from the Speaker.
 
   1. Speaker  -- EFID ------------> Listener   End File
               <------------ EFPA --            Answer YES
 
   2. Speaker  -- EFID ------------> Listener   End File
               <------------ EFPA --            Answer YES   CD
               -- CD -------------->            Change Direction
      Listener <------------ EERP -- Speaker    End to End Response
               -------------- RTR ->            Ready to Receive
      Listener <------------ NERP -- Speaker    Negative End Response
               -------------- RTR ->            Ready to Receive
               Go to Start File Phase
 
   3. Speaker  -- EFID ------------> Listener   End File
               <------------ EFNA --            Answer NO
 
   Following the receipt of a positive End File command which does
   not request a Change Direction command, the Speaker has the option
   to send   a file (SFID), an EERP/NERP, a CD or an ESID with error. 

   If the Speaker wishes to end the session normally, a 
   Change Direction (CD) command MUST be sent to the Listener.
 
   4. Speaker  -- EFID ------------> Listener   End File
               <------------ EFPA --            Answer YES   No CD
               -- CD -------------->            Change Direction
      Listener <------------ ESID -- Speaker    End Session
notes:
This erratum adds a little more documentation to the ODETTE protocol,
but doesn't seem to be correcting an actual error.

orig_text:
The Initiator sends a Security Change Direction (SECD) to which the
   Responder replies with an Authentication Challenge (AUCH).

   The Responder looks up the public certificate that is linked to the
   purported identity of the Initiator (located in the SSID).  If the
   Responder is unable to locate a suitable certificate then
   authentication fails.  The Responder uses the public key contained in
   the certificate to encrypt a random challenge, unique for each
   session, for the Initiator.  This encrypted challenge is sent as a
   [CMS] envelope to the Initiator as part of the AUCH.

   The Initiator decrypts the challenge using their private key and
   sends the decrypted challenge back to the Responder in the
   Authentication Response (AURP).

   The Responder checks that the data received in the AURP matches the
   random challenge that was sent to the Initiator.
correct_text:
The Initiator sends a Security Change Direction (SECD) to which the
   Responder replies with an Authentication Challenge (AUCH).

   The Responder looks up the public certificate that is linked to the
   purported identity of the Initiator (located in the SSID).  If the
   Responder is unable to locate a suitable certificate then
   authentication fails.  The Responder uses the public key contained in
   the certificate to encrypt a random challenge, unique for each
   session, for the Initiator.  This encrypted challenge is sent as a
   [CMS] envelope to the Initiator as part of the AUCH.

   The Initiator decrypts the challenge using their private key and
   sends the decrypted challenge back to the Responder in the
   Authentication Response (AURP).  Because the AUCH CMS envelope
   (Section 5.3.17) and plaintext AURP (Section 5.3.18) do not bind
   the peer's SSIDCODE, role/direction (Initiator vs. Responder), or
   session context, and because the Initiator decrypts an AUCH before
   the Responder has authenticated itself, an Initiator or Responder
   can be exploited as a cross-session decryption oracle unless
   mitigated:
   - An unauthenticated party can forward a victim's AUCH challenge to
     another connection where the certificate holder acts as Initiator
     (Phase 1) or Responder (Phase 2), recovering the decrypted 20-byte
     challenge from AURP and replaying it to impersonate the victim.
   - Because Phase 2 occurs even when the Responder authenticated under
     a different identity (e.g., an attacker's own SSID), an attacker
     can authenticate as itself in Phase 1 and then relay a third
     party's AUCH to the Responder in Phase 2 to obtain a valid AURP
     for that third party's identity.

   To prevent cross-session reflection and decryption-oracle attacks
   within the existing wire format, implementations MUST enforce
   transport-layer mutual authentication (e.g., mutually authenticated
   TLS) binding the peer identity to the presented SSIDCODE before
   performing AUCH/AURP, OR ensure distinct keypairs/certificates are
   used per role/endpoint and reject any incoming AUCH matching an
   outstanding outgoing challenge or arriving in an unexpected state.

   The Responder checks that the data received in the AURP matches the
   random challenge that was sent to the Initiator.
notes:
Methodology & Tooling Disclosure:
I am not claiming personal expertise at the level of formal protocol verification; this submission was heavily assisted by Google Gemini alongside my open-source RFC-LLM pipeline (https://github.com/mariobx/RFC-LLM) and MITRE CPSA 4.4.9 (`cpsa4`). All RFC quotes were verified verbatim against the published .txt specification, and the formal counterexample witnesses were produced mechanically by `cpsa4`, submitted in good faith for Independent Submissions Editor / author review.


RFC 5024 Sections 4.2.4, 5.3.17 (AUCH), and 5.3.18 (AURP) specify a symmetric two-phase challenge-response mutual authentication protocol:
- Phase 1: Responder sends AUCH containing a [CMS]-encrypted 20-byte random challenge under the Initiator's certificate (looked up from SSID), and Initiator returns the decrypted 20-byte challenge in AURP.
- Phase 2: Roles reverse (`<- SECD`, `-> AUCH`, `<- AURP`), using the exact same AUCH/AURP structures.

Three structural cryptographic flaws are present and unaddressed in Sections 4.2.4, 5.3.17, 5.3.18, and 11 (Security Considerations):

1. Missing identity, role, and session binding in AUCH/AURP:
   AUCHCHAL encrypts only the raw 20-byte random number in a bare CMS EnvelopedData without including SSIDCODE of the challenger/peer, role/direction ("Initiator" vs. "Responder"), or a channel/session identifier. AURPRSP returns the raw decrypted 20 bytes in the clear with no MAC or signature.

2. Pre-authentication decryption oracle (Initiator-Initiator reflection):
   In Phase 1, the Initiator decrypts an arbitrary AUCH CMS envelope and returns the plaintext 20 bytes in AURP before the Responder has authenticated. An attacker receiving an AUCH from an honest Responder targeting victim identity A can initiate or accept a session with A (as Initiator), replay the Responder's AUCH to A, obtain AURP from A, and forward AURP to the honest Responder to impersonate A.

3. Cross-identity Phase-2 reflection (Responder-Responder impersonation):
   An attacker using its own valid credentials M can connect to an honest Responder B, complete Phase 1 honestly as M, and then relay a third party A's Phase-2 AUCH challenge (encrypted under B's public key) to B in Phase 2. B decrypts the challenge and hands AURPRSP back to M, allowing M to impersonate B to A even though B only authenticated peer M. Using the same certificate for both Initiator and Responder roles additionally enables same-host Phase-1/Phase-2 reflection.

Formal Verification Evidence:
Automated cryptographic protocol analysis using MITRE CPSA (cpsa4) on the RFC 5024 OFTP2 authentication model (odette-ftp-v2-secure-authentication.scm / odette-ftp-v2-secure-authentication_shapes.txt) verified both same-role reflection attacks:
- Shape label 1 (lines 105-158): Initiator-Initiator same-role reflection / oracle exploitation.
- Shape label 5 (lines 378-443): Responder-Responder same-role reflection / cross-session misbinding.

Supporting model artifacts:
- CPSA model:
  https://github.com/mariobx/Errata-for-RFC-Editor/blob/main/RFC5024/odette-ftp-v2-secure-authentication.scm
- Non-shapes XHTML output:
  https://github.com/mariobx/Errata-for-RFC-Editor/blob/main/RFC5024/odette-ftp-v2-secure-authentication.xhtml
- Shapes XHTML output:
  https://github.com/mariobx/Errata-for-RFC-Editor/blob/main/RFC5024/odette-ftp-v2-secure-authentication_shapes.xhtml

Applicability after RFC 8996: RFC 8996 updates the permitted TLS
versions but does not modify the AUCH/AURP exchange or authentication
state machine in Section 4.2.4. It also does not require binding the
authenticated TLS peer identity to the presented SSIDCODE. Therefore,
the reported reflection and session-binding issue remains applicable
to deployments relying on AUCH/AURP alone or lacking that binding.

Deployment context (keeps the impact claim proportionate):
RFC 5024 is a 2007 Independent Submission (Informational), Updated by
RFC 8996. Where OFTP2 is run over mutually authenticated TLS, the peer
is authenticated before AUCH/AURP and the cross-session reflection and
decryption-oracle behaviors described here are already blocked; the
residual exposure is in deployments that rely on AUCH/AURP alone or
that do not bind the TLS peer identity to the presented SSIDCODE. This
erratum is therefore a documentation/robustness correction, not a claim
that typical deployed OFTP2 is currently exploitable.

Scope Note per IESG / RFC Editor Errata Processing Guidelines:
Modifying AUCHCHAL/AURPRSP to use signed challenges or structured payloads containing both peers' SSIDCODEs, direction flags, and session/TLS-exporter bindings changes the OFTP2 wire format and requires a protocol revision (-bis / OFTP3). The Corrected Text adds a wire-compatible implementation warning and transport/state-machine mitigation to Section 4.2.4. Note that existing "Held for Document Update" errata EID 3453 (Section 4.5.1) and EID 3454 (Section 5.3.2) do not conflict with this erratum, and RFC 5024 was later Updated by RFC 8996 (TLS version deprecation).
